name: Authentication
explanation: Verifying who a user is, for example with a password, a one-time code or a sign-in provider such as Google.
triggers: log in;sign up;password;who the user is;user account;register
requirements: Allow long passwords, at least 64 characters, and reject known breached passwords;Give the same error for a wrong username or a wrong password;Limit repeated failed logins per account and per IP address;Send login forms and session cookies only over HTTPS;Offer two-factor authentication;Require at least 8 characters, or 15 when the password is the only factor;Allow password managers and pasting, and never make a memory test or puzzle the only way to sign in;Never require character mixes or regular password changes, and accept spaces and Unicode
done_when: Login errors never reveal whether an account exists;Repeated wrong passwords are slowed down or blocked

name: Authorization and roles
explanation: Deciding what a signed-in user is allowed to do, usually through roles or permissions.
triggers: admin only;only admins;allowed to;who can see;restrict access;not allowed;who can;can approve;only managers;manager role
requirements: Check permissions on the server for every request, not only by hiding buttons;Deny by default, and give each role only what it needs;Check that the user may access the specific record, not only that they are signed in;Keep permission checks in one shared place instead of copied around;Add automated tests that check each role is refused what it may not do
done_when: Changing an id in the URL never shows another user's data;A user without permission gets 403 even when calling the API directly

name: Password hashing
explanation: Storing passwords as slow, salted hashes (such as bcrypt or Argon2) so they cannot be read if the database leaks.
triggers: store passwords;save passwords;password safely;secure passwords;encrypt password;stored safely;passwords stored;storing passwords
requirements: Hash passwords with Argon2id, scrypt or bcrypt, never plain SHA or MD5;Let the library create a unique salt for every password;Tune the work factor so one hash takes a noticeable fraction of a second;Never log, email or store passwords in plain text;Rehash with stronger settings when users next sign in
done_when: The database contains no readable or reversible passwords;Two users with the same password have different hashes

name: Input sanitization and escaping
explanation: Treating user input as untrusted and escaping or validating it to prevent attacks such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting (XSS).
triggers: hack;malicious input;safe from attacks;user input;security;script tag;html in input;inject;typed code
requirements: Validate input on the server against allowed types, lengths and formats;Use parameterized queries or an ORM, never SQL built from strings;Escape output for where it goes: HTML, attributes, URLs or JavaScript;Avoid innerHTML with user content, or sanitize it with a library such as DOMPurify;Add a Content Security Policy as a second line of defence;Check business rules on the server, such as prices, quantities and step order, never trusting the client;Redirect only to allowed URLs or relative paths, never to any URL taken from the request;Never rely on globals or document properties that user HTML with id or name attributes could override
done_when: Script tags or SQL quotes typed by a user are shown as plain text or rejected;Security scanners find no injection or XSS problems

name: Single sign-on (SSO)
explanation: Letting users sign in with an existing account from a provider such as Google, Microsoft or their company, usually through OAuth or OpenID Connect.
triggers: sign in with google;login with google;google account;microsoft account;github login;company account
requirements: Use a proven OAuth 2.0 or OpenID Connect library instead of writing the flow yourself;Use the authorization code flow with PKCE, and check the state parameter;Verify the ID token's signature, issuer, audience and expiry;Link accounts by the provider's user id, not by email alone;Handle the user cancelling and the provider being unavailable;Send and check a nonce in OpenID Connect sign-ins to stop token replay;For SAML, validate signed assertions with a maintained library, and check audience, recipient, expiry and replay
done_when: Signing in with the provider finds or creates the right account;A forged or expired token is rejected

name: Two-factor authentication (2FA)
explanation: Asking for a second proof of identity after the password, such as a code from an authenticator app, a text message or a security key.
triggers: two factor;code from their phone;verification code;second step;authenticator app;extra security;login code;security key
requirements: Support an authenticator app (TOTP) or passkeys, and treat SMS codes as weaker;Give recovery codes when two-factor is turned on;Rate-limit code attempts;Ask for the password or a code before turning two-factor off;Let users trust a device for a limited time only;Offer a phishing-resistant option, such as passkeys or security keys;Never use email as the second factor
done_when: Signing in on a new device always asks for the second factor;A lost phone can be handled with a recovery code

name: Session management
explanation: Keeping a user signed in between requests with a session or token, and deciding when that ends, for example after inactivity or with a remember-me option.
triggers: logged out;getting logged out;log the user out;stay logged in;remember me;keep me signed in;after inactivity;doing nothing;session expires
requirements: Keep the session in a cookie with HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite set;Create a new session id after login;End sessions after inactivity and after a maximum lifetime;Make logout end the session on the server too;Let users see and end their other sessions;Warn users before a session times out, and let them extend it;Detect signs of a stolen session, such as a sudden IP or device change, and ask the user to sign in again;For sensitive apps, end sessions after about 1 hour idle and 24 hours in total
done_when: After logout, the old session cookie no longer works;Scripts on the page cannot read the session cookie

name: Password reset
explanation: Letting a user who forgot their password choose a new one through a time-limited link sent to their email.
triggers: forgot my password;forgot their password;reset password;change password
requirements: Show the same message whether or not the email has an account;Send a random, single-use link that expires within about an hour;Store only a hash of the reset token;End other sessions after the password changes;Rate-limit reset requests;Build the reset link from a configured base URL, never from the request Host header;Never use security questions or password hints, for sign-in or for account recovery
done_when: Using a reset link twice, or after it expires, fails;The reset form never reveals which emails are registered

name: Email verification
explanation: Confirming that a new user owns their email address by sending a link or code they must click or enter.
triggers: confirm their email;verification link;email is real;activate account;confirm the account
requirements: Send a random, single-use link or code that expires;Explain what to do if the email does not arrive, with a rate-limited resend button;Verify again when the user changes their email address;Limit what unverified accounts can do
done_when: The link verifies the account once, and old links stop working;Resending is possible but limited

name: CSRF protection
explanation: Stopping other websites from submitting forms or requests on behalf of a signed-in user, using anti-forgery tokens and SameSite cookies.
triggers: from another site;forged request;submit forms from;on behalf of the user
requirements: Use the framework's CSRF tokens for every form and state-changing request;Set SameSite=Lax or Strict on session cookies;Never change data in response to GET requests;Check the Origin header on state-changing requests
done_when: A form posted from another website is rejected;Every POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE without a valid CSRF token is rejected

name: HTTPS and TLS
explanation: Encrypting traffic between the browser and the server with a TLS certificate, so the address starts with https and shows a padlock.
triggers: not secure warning;padlock;secure connection;certificate
requirements: Serve every page over HTTPS, and redirect HTTP to HTTPS;Turn on HSTS so browsers always use HTTPS;Renew certificates automatically, for example with Let's Encrypt;Allow only TLS 1.2 and newer;Load all scripts, images and styles over HTTPS too;Allow only strong cipher suites with forward secrecy, such as the Mozilla intermediate configuration
done_when: The browser shows a secure connection with no mixed-content warnings;An SSL test such as SSL Labs gives at least an A grade

name: Cookie consent
explanation: A banner that asks visitors for permission before setting non-essential cookies, as required by laws such as the GDPR.
triggers: accept cookies;cookie popup;privacy law;ask permission;tracking consent
requirements: Set no analytics or marketing cookies before the user agrees;Make rejecting as easy as accepting, on the same screen;Let users change their choice later from a link on every page;Remember the choice and record when consent was given;Explain what each cookie category is for
done_when: Rejecting cookies means no tracking cookies are set;The banner works with the keyboard and with a screen reader

name: Passkeys (WebAuthn)
explanation: Signing in with the device's fingerprint, face or PIN instead of a password, using the WebAuthn standard.
triggers: sign in with fingerprint;login with face id;login without a password;touch id;no password login;windows hello;instead of a password
requirements: Use a maintained WebAuthn library on the server to check registrations and sign-ins;Check the challenge, origin and relying party id on every response;Create a new random challenge for each attempt, and let it expire;Let users register several passkeys, and name and remove them;Keep account recovery as strong as the passkey, not a weak fallback;Accept synced passkeys, and use the backup flags only if policy requires device-bound keys
done_when: Signing in with a passkey works, and a replayed response is rejected;Users can add and remove passkeys from their account

name: Bot protection
explanation: Stopping automated scripts from creating fake accounts, stuffing stolen passwords or spamming forms.
triggers: stop bots;fake sign ups;spam bots;bots signing up;automated attacks;bot traffic;fake accounts
requirements: Rate-limit sign-up, login and other forms that bots target;Show a challenge, such as a CAPTCHA, only when behaviour looks suspicious;Choose an accessible challenge, with an alternative to visual puzzles;Stop credential stuffing by checking breached passwords and unusual sign-in patterns;Add a hidden honeypot field to simple forms;Watch sign-up and login numbers, and alert on sudden spikes
done_when: Scripted mass sign-ups are blocked or slowed down;People using screen readers can still complete the forms

name: Security headers
explanation: HTTP response headers, such as Content Security Policy, that tell browsers how to protect your pages.
triggers: security headers;stop my site being framed;embedded in an iframe;iframe attack;harden the website;browser security;iframe;in an iframe
requirements: Set a Content Security Policy that allows only your own scripts, using nonces or hashes, not unsafe-inline;Stop other sites framing your pages with CSP frame-ancestors, or X-Frame-Options DENY;Send X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff;Set a Referrer-Policy, such as strict-origin-when-cross-origin;Remove headers that reveal software versions, such as X-Powered-By;Set Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy to isolate your pages from other windows;Load third-party scripts and styles with Subresource Integrity
done_when: A header scanner such as securityheaders.com finds CSP, frame-ancestors, nosniff and Referrer-Policy set;Embedding your pages in an iframe on another site is blocked

name: Encrypting sensitive data
explanation: Protecting stored data, such as personal details or tokens, so it stays unreadable if it is stolen.
synonyms: encryption at rest;field encryption;key management;kms;secrets vault
triggers: encrypt data;encrypt sensitive;store sensitive data;protect personal data;encrypt the database;store credit card;keep data safe;id numbers;sensitive information
requirements: Store only the sensitive data you really need;Encrypt sensitive data at rest with a standard algorithm, such as AES-GCM, from a well-known library;Keep keys in a key management service or vault, separate from the data, and rotate them;Never invent your own cryptography, and never use ECB mode, MD5 or SHA-1 for security;Give the app's database user only the rights it needs, and keep the database off the public internet;Hash passwords instead of encrypting them
done_when: Stolen database files or backups reveal no readable sensitive data;No plaintext keys are in the code, the repository or the database

name: Dependency security
explanation: Keeping the libraries, packages and third-party scripts your app uses free of known vulnerabilities and tampering.
triggers: vulnerable packages;outdated dependencies;update dependencies;third party scripts;npm packages;libraries are safe;malicious package
requirements: Commit a lock file, and install exactly from it in CI, such as with npm ci;Scan dependencies for known vulnerabilities automatically, and update promptly;Check new packages before adding them: maintenance, popularity and the exact name, to avoid typosquatting;Pin CI actions to full commit hashes, and build tools to exact versions;Load third-party scripts with Subresource Integrity, or host them yourself;Produce a software bill of materials (SBOM) for each release;Remove dependencies you no longer use
done_when: The build fails or warns on dependencies with known critical vulnerabilities;Every dependency version is fixed by the lock file

name: Injection prevention
explanation: Keeping user input from being run as code or commands, in SQL, shell commands, templates, XML and more.
synonyms: command injection;nosql injection;xxe;template injection;prototype pollution;insecure deserialization
triggers: run a shell command;user input in a query;build a sql query;parse xml;eval user input;execute a command;unserialize
requirements: Use parameterized queries or an ORM for every database query, including NoSQL filters;Never pass user input to a shell, and run programs with an argument list instead;Never pass user input to eval, template compilers or other dynamic code;Turn off external entities and DTDs in XML parsers;Never deserialize untrusted data with native formats such as pickle or Java serialization;Escape user input in LDAP and XPath queries, or avoid building them from strings;Block __proto__, constructor and prototype keys when merging user JSON into objects;Run the database and services with the fewest privileges they need
done_when: Injection payloads in every input are treated as plain data;Security scanners find no injection problems

name: Fetching URLs safely (SSRF)
explanation: Letting the server fetch a URL a user supplies, such as for link previews, without exposing internal systems.
triggers: fetch a url;link preview;import from a url;load an image from a url;user enters a url;download from a link;url preview;pastes a link;paste a link;preview of a link
requirements: Allow only http and https, and only the hosts you expect where possible;Resolve the host, block private, loopback, link-local and metadata IPs, and connect only to the IP you checked (DNS rebinding);Check every redirect the same way, or turn redirects off;Set short timeouts and a maximum response size;Send these requests from an isolated network or proxy without access to internal services
done_when: A URL pointing at localhost, an internal address or the cloud metadata address is refused;A redirect to an internal address is refused too

name: Privacy and personal data
explanation: Handling people's personal data lawfully and carefully, as laws such as the GDPR require.
synonyms: data protection;privacy;personal data;ccpa;right to be forgotten
triggers: delete my account;export my data;personal information;privacy policy;user data;data retention;anonymize data;delete their account;delete account;all their data
requirements: Collect only the personal data you need, and explain why in a privacy notice;Let users download their data and delete their account;Delete or anonymize personal data when it is no longer needed;Limit who can access personal data, and log that access;Keep personal data out of logs, analytics and error reports;Check where third-party services store the data you send them;Ask for device permissions only when needed, and never track users with hardware identifiers
done_when: Deleting an account removes or anonymizes the user's personal data everywhere, backups on schedule;Users can download a copy of their data
